interviewQuestions.question: Why does Android's ViewModel exist, and what problem did it actually solve?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Before `ViewModel`, surviving a rotation meant manually shuttling everything through `onSaveInstanceState`'s Bundle — workable for a scroll position, genuinely painful for a screen's full presentation state: loaded data, in-flight requests, validation state. Every screen ended up with its own ad hoc, inconsistent survival logic, and getting it wrong meant a form clearing or a list re-fetching on every rotation.

`ViewModel` solves it structurally rather than by convention: Android retains the **same instance** across the Activity being destroyed and recreated specifically for a configuration change, and hands that same instance to the new Activity. From the `ViewModel`'s own perspective, the rotation essentially didn't happen — it was never destroyed, so anything it holds simply survives without any explicit save/restore code.

The scoping mechanism matters for the boundary case: a `ViewModel` is retrieved through a scope tied to an owner — an Activity, a Fragment, a nav graph destination. As long as that owner survives the recreation (true for a config change, false when the user genuinely navigates away and the scope is cleared), the same instance comes back; once the scope is actually cleared, `onCleared()` fires and the `ViewModel` is genuinely gone, which is the right time to cancel any ongoing work tied to it.

**Testing:** whether you understand ViewModel as solving configuration-change survival specifically, not just "a place to put business logic."

interviewQuestions.question: A ViewModel has three separate StateFlow properties — isLoading, error, and data — updated somewhat independently across different code paths. QA reports a screen briefly showing both a loading spinner and an error message at the same time. How do you fix this?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
This is the textbook symptom of partial-state inconsistency that comes from splitting one screen's state across several independently-updated observable properties instead of one single state object — there's a brief window where `isLoading` has been reset to false and `data` hasn't been set yet, but `error` from a previous attempt hasn't been cleared, and the UI, which reads all three independently, renders a combination that was never intended to be reachable together.

The fix is consolidating into a single sealed state type — `Loading`, `Success(data)`, `Error(message)` — exposed as one `StateFlow<UiState>`, updated atomically in one assignment rather than three separate property writes. Because the UI now reads one value and does an exhaustive `when` over it, an inconsistent combination like "loading and error simultaneously" becomes structurally unrepresentable — there's no state value that means both at once.

This is essentially borrowing MVI's core discipline (one immutable state object per screen, updated via a single reducer-style assignment) without needing to adopt the rest of MVI's machinery — a sealed class plus a single `StateFlow` gets most of the benefit. I'd also audit for the same pattern on other screens in the codebase, since if one `ViewModel` accumulated several independent flags, it's a good bet the pattern was copied elsewhere too.

**Testing:** whether you can diagnose a state-consistency bug back to its architectural root cause and propose a specific, minimal-disruption fix rather than patching the symptom with an extra flag.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you structure the Repository layer for a screen that needs to work offline-first — show cached data immediately, then update once fresh data arrives?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd have the Repository return a `Flow` that can emit more than once for a single logical request: first the currently cached value from the local database immediately (so the UI has something to show with zero latency), then trigger a network fetch in the background, write the fresh result into the local database, and let the same Flow (now observing that database, not a one-shot network call) emit the updated value automatically once the write completes.

Concretely, the Repository composes two things: a `Flow` from Room that observes the relevant table (so any future writes to it automatically re-emit to every observer, not just this one call), and a background coroutine that performs the network fetch and writes into that same table when it succeeds. The `ViewModel` never needs to know this is happening — it just collects one `Flow<User>` and gets an immediate cached value followed naturally by a fresher one, with no special-casing on the calling side.

The part worth being explicit about in the interview: what happens on network failure. The cached value should still be showing, and the failure needs a path to reach the `ViewModel` — often a separate result/error signal alongside the data `Flow`, since the data `Flow`'s job is just "what's the current best-known value," not error reporting for a specific fetch attempt. Conflating the two makes the state model harder to reason about later.

This is also exactly where the Repository pattern earns its abstraction — the `ViewModel` and View never change regardless of whether this is a pure-network fetch, a pure-cache read, or this full offline-first strategy; the decision lives entirely inside the Repository.

**Testing:** whether you can design a concrete offline-first data flow, not just recite that Repository "decides between cache and network."

interviewQuestions.question: As a staff engineer, how would you evaluate whether a team's MVVM implementation is actually giving them the benefits of the pattern, versus just following its naming conventions?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd look past whether classes are named `ViewModel` and `Repository` and check whether the actual dependency and testing structure the pattern is supposed to buy is really there, because it's entirely possible to have the right class names with none of the real discipline.

Concretely: can every `ViewModel` in the codebase be unit-tested with zero real I/O — no real network calls, no real database — by injecting a fake `Repository`? If a meaningful fraction of `ViewModel`s can't be tested that way because they're calling a network client or a DAO directly, the Repository abstraction exists in name for some screens and not others, which usually means the team adopted the pattern's vocabulary without enforcing its actual boundary.

Second: is there ever more than one observable state property per screen that can independently drift — `isLoading`/`error`/`data` as three separate flows rather than one sealed state? That's a sign the "View" side of MVVM is technically true (a ViewModel exposes observable state) but the single-source-of-truth discipline that makes MVVM valuable isn't actually being enforced.

Third: does any `ViewModel` hold a reference back to a View or Activity, even indirectly through a callback captured at construction time? That's the clearest sign the unidirectional-flow boundary has been violated somewhere, usually under time pressure on a screen that needed to do something the clean pattern didn't obviously support, and it's worth specifically auditing for.

I'd treat all three as a lightweight audit checklist for any codebase claiming to use MVVM, precisely because "we use MVVM" as a description tells you very little on its own — the actual boundaries and discipline are what determine whether the codebase gets the pattern's real benefits or just its file-naming convention.

**Testing:** whether you can look past surface-level pattern adoption and assess whether the actual architectural benefits — testability, single source of truth, dependency inversion — are genuinely present.
